entry.title: The Shape of Growth: Tracing African Urbanisation

link.title: The Shape of Growth: Tracing African Urbanisation

entry.content:
Most people outside the continent imagine African life as rural life. That image is inaccurate and outdated, and becoming more so every year. Africa was the last continent to urbanise, but it is now doing so at breakneck speed, faster than any other. Today nearly three-quarters of Africans live in urban or semi-urban settings.1 Over the next three decades Africa’s urban population will double, from about 700 million to 1.4 billion with two out of three Africans living in urban areas by 2050, making it the continent with the second-largest urban population after Asia.1 2.

Is this good news? Well, it depends. City life can improve people’s lives materially, change social and political attitudes,3 and make a less carbon-intensive lifestyle possible.4 But whether it does all that depends on the type of urbanisation. So let’s take a closer look at the shape of this remarkable growth.

Motivated by this great piece in the Financial Times and World Cities Day, I tracked the growth of built-up land and population in Africa’s 100 largest cities between 1990 and 2025, using data from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), Open Street Map (OSM) and nighttime lights data captured by satelittes.5 6 For each city I hold its boundary fixed at its 2020 Africapolis outline and measure what happens inside it over time. The sample includes megacities like Lagos, Cairo and Nairobi, but also places like Osogbo, Mwanza and Bafoussam: cities of more than a million people that many outside the continent will never have heard of.

What the data show

Between 1990 and 2025, the built-up area of Africa’s 100 largest cities grew from about 6,900 to 12,500 km², an increase of 81%. Over the same period their population went from 142 to 370 million, an increase of 161%. By 2025, 89 of these cities had more than a million inhabitants, twice as many million-plus cities as Latin America. The chart below puts each city’s population and built-up land on the same scale, both starting at 100 in 1990. Where the people line (blue) ends above the built-up land line (orange), construction did not keep pace with population growth.

Population and built-up land, 1990 = 100 (log scale)
Show as a table
In 74 of Africa's 100 largest cities, population grew faster than built-up land.

So in most of the cities in our sample, 74 of the 100, population has grown faster than urban land. There are exceptions. Kigali, a city that has invested heavily in planned expansion, roads and serviced land under its citywide master plan, is one example. Juba, the capital of South Sudan, is a tragic one, where the civil war has caused major displacement. But in the median city, each million residents now live on 35 km² of built-up land, down from 48 km² in 1990. Within their boundaries, African cities have become markedly denser. But denser does not mean compact. More people per square kilometre of built-up land tells us nothing about where the new buildings went. As we will see, even inside the boundaries most new construction went onto empty land at the edge rather than filling in existing neighbourhoods. And beyond their boundaries, cities have spread further out creating peri-urban zones and satelitte towns.

The promise of density

Economic historians and political scientists have long pointed out that Africa has historically been held back by its relatively low population densities.7 8 Ask the economic consultants and they will point to the growth opportunities that come with a growing population. More people, more demand, more growth is the simplified logic. Beyond pure demand, should you ever enter a seminar room full of economists (especially the urban and economic-geography types), make sure “agglomeration economies” is on your bingo card. The idea has a long history in the discipline, running all the way back to Alfred Marshall’s Principles of Economics, published in 1890.9 Firms that cluster in cities gain access to a larger labour market, to specialised inputs and to more potential trading partners, and they benefit from knowledge spillovers: Marshall’s “ideas in the air”. Jane Jacobs later added that it is the sheer variety of activity in cities, not only the concentration of a single industry, that breeds new ideas.10 These productivity gains show up in the income gap between cities and the countryside,11 and the urban wage premium in low- and middle-income countries holds up under careful testing.12 The “growth miracles” of East Asia are unimaginable without urbanisation: in China, the urban population grew by 700 million people between 1978 and 2009, while GDP per person rose thirteen-fold.13

Denser, but spreading out

African cities do produce some of these gains, if modest ones: across 2,600 cities in 34 countries, a 10% increase in population density raises productivity by 0.2–0.5%, with most estimates at the lower end.2 But these gains depend on good spatial connectivity: workers need to be able to reach jobs, and firms each other. And even inside their boundaries, cities did not grow mainly by filling in. The GHSL data let us distinguish new construction on land that was already partly built up (“infill”) from construction on previously empty, greenfield land. Taking all 100 cities together, around 58% of new construction since 1990 went onto greenfield land. Greenfield construction is a lot more common in East (68%) and West Africa (60%) than in Southern (42%) and North African cities (47%), and the same ranking holds for the typical city in each region, shown below.

Share of new construction on greenfield land: the typical city in each region, 1990–2025
Show as a table

Greenfield does not mean empty. Land at the edge of a city is usually already doing something: growing food for the city, or holding trees and bush that shade it, soak up heavy rain and store carbon. So what did all this new construction replace? Matching each newly built pixel to a 1990 land-cover map gives a rough answer.

What the new greenfield construction was built on: land cover in 1990, share of built-up added 1990–2025

Land cover from GLC_FCS30D (30 m, 1990). "Tree cover" includes tree-rich farmland and bush as well as forest. "Other" is mostly land the land-cover map already shows as built-up, plus water and wetland.

Show as a table

Across all cities, almost half of the new greenfield construction went onto tree cover, mostly tree-rich farmland and bush rather than forest, and about a quarter onto cropland. The mix varies by region. In West Africa, two-thirds replaced tree cover. In North Africa, where farmland is scarce, nearly half came out of cropland and most of the rest out of desert.

Building height fell in 99 of the 100 cities. Not one got taller.

As a result of this outward sprawl, average building height across African cities has actually decreased, not increased: the median city’s mean building height slipped from 7.7 m to 7.3 m between 2000 and 2025. In fact, not one city saw an increase. Height fell in 99 of the 100 cities and stayed flat in Lomé.14 Sprawl of this kind complicates infrastructure provision, and as a result many African cities are spatially dispersed and lack connectivity, leaving residents cut off from jobs and basic services such water, sanitation and waste management.11 One World Bank study finds the average African city about 20% more fragmented than cities in Asia, with 37% less exposure to people and jobs.15 What is more, African cities are, perhaps surprisingly, expensive cities. Households face costs about 29% higher than in other countries at similar income levels,15 and housing in sub-Saharan Africa is about 55% more expensive than in other low-income countries.16

Satellite towns and peri-urbanisation

And all of these numbers count only what happens inside each city’s fixed boundary. Step outside it and the sprawl is larger still: cities are consuming an ever-larger footprint of land, much of it beyond their official limits, creating mushrooming peri-urban zones and satelitte towns with poor connectivity and infrastructure access. The animations below show seven examples: Addis Ababa, Ouagadougou and Kigali growing outwards in rings, Cairo adding new towns in the desert, Lagos spreading inland from the coast, Kinshasa pushing east and south-west from a core that was already built up by 1990, and Johannesburg filling in and spreading across a sprawling, many-centred region. In Addis Ababa, roughly 140 km² of new built-up land lies just outside the city’s official boundary, about two-thirds as much again as the growth inside it.

A rough test with OpenStreetMap data points the same way. In seven cities where the map coverage is good enough to try (Lagos, Kinshasa, Kampala, Dar es Salaam, Khartoum, Juba and Mogadishu), residents of newly built areas at the edge live farther from the nearest mapped school, clinic or water point than residents of areas that densified: about 20% farther in Lagos, around 60% in Kampala and Mogadishu, and more than twice as far in Kinshasa.17

Urbanisation without industrialisation

Moreover, African urbanisation appears to be driven by different forces. Elsewhere, people moved to cities as economies shifted from farming to manufacturing. In Africa, however, urbanisation seems to follow different rules: it is less driven by this kind of structural transformation. Many African countries have urbanised with little growth in manufacturing,13 and unlike China, Africa has urbanised without major increases in agricultural or industrial productivity.11 Resource-rich countries in particular have produced what Gollin, Jedwab and Vollrath call “consumption cities”, where most jobs are in local trade and services rather than in productive, internationally competitive sectors.18 In fact, much of the growth is not driven by migration at all. Today, most of the increase in Africa’s urban population comes from births exceeding deaths in the cities themselves, rather than from people moving in from the countryside.19 20 Cities are growing whether or not the jobs are there. Without the jobs that industrialisation brings, the benefits of density are harder to realise, and the costs of poorly connected sprawl are harder to bear.

The infrastructure gap

Some basic services appear to be catching up. Nighttime-lights satellite data, admittedly not a perfect proxy, suggests that electrification is spreading fast in most African cities: the dark-or-dim share of built-up area fell from 92% to 5% in Mogadishu, 69% to 2% in Ikorodu, and 82% to 2% in Mwanza between 2000 and 2025, largely in the same fast-growing secondary cities.

Share of built-up area that is dark or only dimly lit at night, 2000 and 2025

Corrected DMSP nighttime lights (DN scale): "dark or dim" means no detectable light or a digital number of 10 or below. Share of 100 m built-up cells within each city's Africapolis boundary. Cities whose boundary takes in large rural areas are left out.

Show as a table

Lights are not the whole story, though. In Afrobarometer’s latest surveys across 39 countries, almost all urban neighbourhoods (94%) had an electricity grid, but only 65% of urban residents said their power works most or all of the time.21 Only about half of urban neighbourhoods had a sewage system, half of urban households had no toilet inside the home, and one in five urban residents had repeatedly gone without enough clean water in the past year.22

In Onitsha, 87% of built-up land is still dark or barely lit at night.

These numbers are indicative and show that a substantial infrastructure gap remains. Where it persists, congestion and pollution rather than ideas will float the air. In 2020, African countries committed only 3.4% of GDP to infrastructure from all sources, about half the rate in South Asia, and more than 30% of what governments budget for infrastructure typically goes unspent.2 Public investment amounts to around USD 104 per person a year (in PPP), against a global average of USD 822.2. And the pressure is likely to grow. Fast growing cities face the highest risks of fragility characterised by inequality, youth unemployment and criminal violence23. What is more, Africa is warming slightly faster than the global average, by about 0.3 °C per decade since 1991, and fastest in the north.24 Many of its largest cities sit on the coast or on iver floodplains. The number of Africans exposed to sea-level rise is projected to double from 54 million in 2000 to 108–116 million by 2030, and to reach 190–245 million by 2060; Lagos, Dar es Salaam, Cotonou and Alexandria are among the most exposed.25.

At the same time, much of the continent’s urban fabric does not exist yet: by one estimate, two-thirds of Africa’s cities are yet to be built.12 That makes the choices made now unusually consequential. Cities in developing countries are among the places most exposed to climate change, but they are also the most viable way of managing its impacts.4 Density cuts emissions per person from infrastructure and services, and taller buildings are less carbon-intensive, which makes the fall in building height described above all the more worrying. Access to local public goods and services also helps households cope with environmental shocks. And what gets built today will last: urban infrastructure typically stays in use for around 125 years and buildings for around 175, so today’s decisions about a city’s physical shape will lock in its costs and emissions for generations.4

What can be done

Beyond a lack of investment, there is a lack of city planning and inefficient land use,2 and vested interests that resist change. City governments are poorly placed to close the gap. Municipalities are cash-strapped, with low tax revenues, and they often lack the political discretion and financial autonomy to raise money on financial markets. Dakar is a case in point: in 2015 the city’s planned CFA 20 billion (about €30 million) municipal bond, backed by a USAID guarantee and a credit rating, was blocked at the last minute by the national government, amid a long-running political conflict between the city and the state.2 26 27 There are signs of change. In 2025 the African Development Bank lent Johannesburg ZAR 2.5 billion (about US$139 million), its first loan to an African city without a national government guarantee.28

  • Planning and zoning: plan for expansion before it happens.
  • City financing: give cities the revenue base and the autonomy to borrow.

Explore all 100 cities

To dig deeper into any of the 100 cities, explore the Urban Africa app I built alongside this post. It has interactive maps of built-up growth and nighttime lights for each city, time series you can compare across cities, and rankings of how they grew.

Data and caveats

Built-up area and population come from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL BUILT-S and GHS-POP, release R2023A, European Commission JRC), in five-year epochs from 1990 to 2025. Values between epochs are interpolated linearly for the animation. City boundaries are Africapolis 2020 agglomerations (OECD/SWAC), held fixed at their 2020 extent for all years. Building height is GHSL BUILT-V (volume) divided by BUILT-S (footprint), available 2000–2025. Nighttime-lights figures use a bloom- and top-coding-corrected DMSP series, also read from 2000. In the footprint animations, an area counts as built up if at least 10% of it is covered by buildings.

Two caveats are worth keeping in mind. Because the boundaries are fixed, growth that spills past them is not counted, so land growth is understated for cities that have outgrown their mapped area. Kinshasa and Luanda had already spread beyond theirs by 1990, and Addis Ababa has since (see above). Africapolis defines an agglomeration physically, as at least 10,000 people in a continuous built-up area with less than 200 metres between buildings, so scattered construction beyond that distance falls outside the boundary by design. And for several smaller cities, the large percentage changes partly reflect how the boundary polygon was drawn rather than actual growth. [TODO: add that the 2025 built-up layer is a model projection rather than an observation, so the final five years likely understate land growth.]

The land-cover breakdown matches each greenfield pixel (GHSL built-up zero in 1990, positive in 2025) to the GLC_FCS30D land-cover map for 1990 (Zhang et al., 30 m resolution), weighted by the built-up surface added. It covers 98 of the 100 cities.29

entry.summary: Africa's largest cities more than doubled their population since 1990 but added far less land. An interactive look at how 100 cities grew, using GHSL built-up and population data.

entry.title: Mapping Conflict in Ethiopia with ACLED Data

link.title: Mapping Conflict in Ethiopia with ACLED Data

entry.content:
Ethiopia has experienced some of the most intense and geographically varied political violence on the continent over the past two decades. This post uses data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) to chart how conflict has unfolded across the country since 2005 — from the protest waves of the mid-2010s to the devastating Tigray War that began in late 2020.

Conflict Trends Over Time

ACLED records political violence and protest events at the individual incident level, allowing us to track not only how many events occurred in a given year but also what types of violence they involved. The charts below focus on four event categories: Battles, Violence against civilians, Protests, and Riots — the types most relevant for studying civil conflict and popular mobilisation.

Number of Events

Two distinct peaks are visible. The first, concentrated in the Protests and Riots panels, corresponds to the Oromo and Amhara protest movement of 2015–2017 that ultimately led to the resignation of Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn and Abiy Ahmed’s rise to power. The second, far larger peak in the Battles and Violence against civilians panels, marks the Tigray War from November 2020.

Reported Fatalities

The fatality data amplify the Tigray signal further. The battles panel shows a catastrophic spike in 2021–2022, consistent with independent estimates placing the war’s death toll in the hundreds of thousands. Violence against civilians fatalities also rose sharply over the same period, reflecting widespread atrocities documented by the UN and human rights organisations.

Where Did the Violence Happen?

To answer the spatial question, the ACLED point events are joined to wereda (district) polygons from the IPUMS Ethiopia shapefile. Weredas with no recorded events in a given year are assigned a count of zero so the maps render without gaps.

Battles and Violence against Civilians, 2020–2024

In 2020 and 2021 fighting was concentrated almost exclusively in Tigray. By 2022 the front had expanded into Amhara and Afar as the conflict escalated into a full-scale multi-front war. The Pretoria Agreement of November 2022 brought a ceasefire that is reflected in the sharp reduction in event counts for 2023 and 2024.

The fatality maps reveal a different pattern from raw event counts: some weredas record relatively few events but extremely high fatality tolls, pointing to particularly lethal engagements or mass atrocities rather than sustained low-level fighting.

Protests and Riots, 2015–2017

Protests and riots in this period were heavily concentrated in Oromia — particularly in the zones surrounding Addis Ababa where the Addis Ababa Integrated Development Master Plan sparked the initial unrest. The movement broadened in 2016 to include Amhara protesters in the north.

Data: ACLED. Administrative boundaries: IPUMS Ethiopia.

entry.title: Has Globalisation Brought About the Death of Distance?

link.title: Has Globalisation Brought About the Death of Distance?

entry.content:
Written as part of GY 409 – Globalisation and Regional Development, MSc Local Economic Development, London School of Economics and Political Science (2018–2019).

“The Death of Distance”, “The World is Flat” or “The Borderless World” - commentators in the financial and economic press have found metaphors aplenty to describe the levelling effects of globalisation. And who could deny that the advances in transport and communication technology have brought humanity closer together? Goods and services are traded across the globe, firms have internationalised, and the spread of the internet allows people to communicate in real time despite being thousands of miles away from each other. Beyond that, numerous trade agreements and supranational organisations have led to an unprecedented harmonisation of policies and regulations across countries. As a result, the sovereignty of the Westphalian nation-state has come under fire as the world ushered an era of “hyperglobalisation”. Hence, it seems straightforward to argue that globalisation has brought about the “death of distance”. But I will argue that this judgment was premature and lacks rigour. On closer inspection, distance still matters a great deal and globalisation has not brought about its death.

To begin with, let us look at the two most important ways in which globalisation might have reduced the effect of distance. First, the past 100 years have seen massive improvements in technology which have reduced costs for transport and communication substantially and integrated hitherto unconnected parts of the world into the global economy. The cost of shipping goods around the globe has reduced by more than 70% since 1920 (Combes et al., 2008). The number of airline passengers has increased from 310 million in 1970 to 4.4 billion in 2019. Finally, the global share of individuals using the internet has skyrocketed from 6% in 2000 to 49% in 2017. These trends are not exclusive to high-income countries. In fact, internet usage in Kenya is now 70 times higher than it was in the early 2000s (World Bank, 2021). Second, trade and financial liberalisation as well as the foundation of supranational organisations have pushed back nation-state sovereignty and brought about institutional levelling. The foundation of the WTO in 1995 extended trade liberalisation far beyond tariff reductions and led to a harmonisation of regulations in areas such as intellectual property rights or health and safety standards (Rodrik, 2018). Financial deregulation and the abolition of capital controls globalised financial markets and meant that investors and stockbrokers were now longer constrained to their domestic economies. These harmonisation efforts found their apex in the EU, where the completion of the “Single Market” project effectuated the “four freedoms of movement” – goods, services, people, and money (Chang, 2014). Indeed, it seems as if both forces worked their magic to reduce the effect of distance. There has been a substantial increase in trade volumes and FDI flows since the 1990s. Moreover, increased mobility and communication have contributed to the dispersion of ideas, knowledge, and technology. So, has globalisation really brought about the death of distance? Not so fast. If that was the case, why don’t we see rapid convergence in technological innovation and living standards across the world? Why do the chances of benefitting from globalisation still vary so widely for different economies and different individuals (Rodríguez-Pose, 2008)? Because distance still matters in the 21st century – let me explain why.

It is a well-established fact in the economics literature that trade, FDI and capital flows decrease with distance. It has been estimated that a 10 percent increase in distance reduces trade volumes by 10 percent. Perhaps surprisingly, a study by Disdier and Head finds that the negative effect of distance on trade has increased since the 1960s (Disdier, 2008). This finding demonstrates two things. First, despite the reduction of transport and communication costs and substantial efforts to harmonise regulations, transaction costs resulting from linguistic and cultural differences remain stubbornly high. Second, there has been a profound economic shift towards more innovative and creative industries in which business networks and relationships arising from proximity matter a great deal. Except for a few long-established manufacturing sectors such as textiles, furniture and simple consumer goods, industries are not nearly as “footloose” as has been suggested. As Ed Leamer puts it, distance still matters because it “creates cost-advantaged relationships between sellers and buyers located close to one another” (Leamer, 2007). The draught horses of the global economy cluster in a few regions with favourable conditions and draw on the benefits of agglomeration economies, thereby increasing the effects of distance. Innovation in the pharmaceutical sector and the software industry, two sectors that have benefitted massively from globalisation, requires not only highly skilled workers and good institutions but trust and cooperation - things that are still much harder to build across the globe than with co-workers next door. As a result, patenting is more concentrated than ever before. And while numerous Asian countries have experienced substantial increases in living standards, least developed countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa were virtually left out. At the same time, interpersonal and regional inequalities within countries have increased across the globe (Bourguignon, 2015). On the political front, the “death of distance” narrative often went hand in hand with a swansong of the nation-state. This too has been belied by the facts. According to the World Values Survey, people across the world still feel much more attached to their respective nations than to the global community. This holds true even for the EU, despite all the efforts put into forging a European identity. Finally, the place of birth remains the most important determinant for predicting a person’s income and explains 60% of the total variation in global income levels (Clemens, 2008).

In conclusion, I have demonstrated that globalisation has not brought about the proclaimed “death of distance”. Undoubtedly, globalisation has connected people across the globe. It also contributed to pull millions of people out of poverty. And yes, it has reduced the distance between a few select metropolitan areas across the globe - connecting Mumbai and Beijing with London and San Francisco. But for people in rural India, Western China and the American Midwest, these places seem more distant than ever before.

References

  • Bourguignon, F. (2015). The Globalisation of Inequality. Princeton University Press.
  • Chang, H.-J. (2014). Economics: The User’s Guide. Pelican Books.
  • Clemens, M. (2008). The place premium: Wage differences for identical workers across the US border. NBER Working Paper.
  • Combes, P.-P., Mayer, T., & Thisse, J.-F. (2008). Economic Geography: The Integration of Regions and Nations. Princeton University Press.
  • Disdier, A.-C., & Head, K. (2008). The puzzling persistence of the distance effect on bilateral trade. Review of Economics and Statistics, 90(1), 37–48.
  • Leamer, E. (2007). A flat world, a level playing field, a small world after all, or none of the above? Journal of Economic Literature, 45(1), 83–126.
  • Rodrik, D. (2018). Straight Talk on Trade: Ideas for a Sane World Economy. Princeton University Press.
  • Rodríguez-Pose, A. (2008). The rise of the “city-region” concept and its development policy implications. European Planning Studies, 16(8), 1025–1046.

entry.summary: Despite falling transport costs, digital connectivity, and sweeping trade liberalisation, this essay argues that distance remains a stubborn and powerful force shaping economic opportunity in the 21st century.

entry.title: Populism and Deindustrialisation: Trade Liberalisation or Technological Change?

link.title: Populism and Deindustrialisation: Trade Liberalisation or Technological Change?

entry.content:
Written as part of GY 409 – Globalisation and Regional Development, MSc Local Economic Development, London School of Economics and Political Science (2018–2019).

The rise of right-wing populism in high-income countries is one of the most pressing issues of our time. Donald Trump, the Brexit advocates, and right-wing parties like the AfD in Germany have all build their campaigns on anti-immigration and anti-globalisation rhetoric. What explains their success? Empirical evidence suggests that support for populist parties is particularly strong in regions that have suffered from declines in manufacturing employment and falling wages – a phenomenon that has been described as the revenge of the places that don’t matter (Rodríguez-Pose, 2018). There is, for example, Saxony - a lagging region of eastern Germany where the AfD obtained 27% of the votes in 2017. There also is West Virginia, a former industrial state in decline, where 68% of people voted for Donald Trump in 2020. These findings raise important questions about the reasons for the decline in manufacturing wages and employment. Are the anti-globalisation campaigners right to blame trade liberalisation? Or is technological change the more important force to consider?

For most of the 20th century, a strong manufacturing sector represented the backbone of economic success in Western Europe and Northern America. Especially during the boom years after World War II, the manufacturing sector spurred growth and created equitable wealth by employing large numbers of low-skilled workers productively. At its peak, during the 1960s, manufacturing employed around 40% of the total workforce in high-income countries. But the heyday of western manufacturing ended sometime during the 1970s, as two stylised facts suggest:

  1. Employment levels in manufacturing fell substantially in all high-income economies. For example, in the UK, the share of manufacturing employment fell from 22% in 1981 to 8% in 2019.
  2. Real wages of low-skilled manufacturing workers in high-income economies have declined between 1980 and 2019.

What explains this development? Trade liberalisation has become a major culprit in the political debate. At first glance, the underlying reasoning is compelling. The 1980s and 1990s saw significant reductions of trade barriers following the foundation of the World Trade Organization and the entrance of China and India into the world economy. As a result, the global labour market grew by millions of low-skilled workers offering their labour at very low wages. According to the classical Hecksher-Ohlin trade model, downward pressure on low-skilled manufacturing wages in high income economies is precisely what we should expect following these events (Bourguignon, 2015). For high-income economies, the model predicts that trade with low-income economies increases the returns to capital and high-skilled labour while it reduces the returns to low-skilled labour (Harrison et al., 2010). And indeed, China’s emergence to becoming a manufacturing powerhouse was promoted by offshoring of light manufacturing industries requiring low skills such as electronics assembly, textiles, and other consumer goods. While this generated substantial aggregate efficiency gains and raised consumer welfare in high-income economies, manufacturing industries at the lower end of the skills spectrum and the regions in which they were located were hit hard by greater exposure to imports. The effects were aggravated by the fact that labour market adjustments in terms of geographical and sectoral mobility were much more sluggish than economists had anticipated (Autor et al., 2016).

Does that mean anti-globalisation campaigners are right in putting all the blame for the decline of manufacturing employment on trade liberalisation? The short answer is no. There are empirical and conceptual issues with this narrative and I will argue that technological change plays a more important role. To begin with, this view neglects the fact that some manufacturing industries have benefitted substantially from the possibility to source inputs at low-cost from abroad bringing about positive aggregate employment effects. Think, for example, of the automotive industry in Germany. Secondly, manufacturing employment peaked during the 1960s and was therefore falling already long before China’s accession to the WTO in 2001 impacted trade volumes substantially. Most importantly however and often overlooked, is the fact that total manufacturing output in high-income economies has constantly grown, even in the United Kingdom, a country notorious for its declining productive sector. This means that a large part of the reduction in manufacturing employment is explained by increasing productivity because of technological innovation rather than import competition. In fact, technological innovation has been a double whammy for low-skilled workers in the Saxonies’ and the West Virginia’s of this world. It did not only reduce the number of manufacturing jobs, but it did so especially at the expense of workers without college degrees. This phenomenon is called skill-biased technological change and has led to increasing wage returns to human capital and job polarisation as a result (Katz, 2008). For the manufacturing sector, this means increasing demand for engineers and reduced demand and falling wages for workers undertaking routine tasks on the assembly line. Importantly, this is not to say that trade liberalisation did not play a role in this process. More competition on international markets increased pressure among manufacturing firms to innovate and thereby accelerated technological change (Bourguignon, 2015). But the point I am making is that technological change is the most important reason behind declining manufacturing employment and falling wages for low-skilled workers.

In conclusion, import competition did indeed have localised effects on certain sectors and regions. The grievances are real, and the socioeconomic consequences were particularly severe in countries with poor social safety nets like the United States. This might explain why trade with China played such a prominent role in Donald Trump’s campaign while it was absent in that of the AfD in Germany. Nevertheless, I have shown that manufacturing employment was on the decline a long time before trade with low-income countries intensified. Most importantly, the fact that total manufacturing output has been increasing across all high-income economies strongly suggests that technological innovation is the main reason behind the reduction in manufacturing employment. Therefore, to really help the places that don’t matter, the policy focus should be on promoting more inclusive technological innovation, improving education systems and strengthening social safety nets. Trumpist’ protectionism, in contrast, was a knee-jerk reaction to a problem poorly understood.

References

  • Autor, D., Dorn, D., & Hanson, G. (2016). The China shock: Learning from labor market adjustment to large changes in trade. Annual Review of Economics, 8, 205–240.
  • Bourguignon, F. (2015). The Globalisation of Inequality. Princeton University Press.
  • Harrison, A., McLaren, J., & McMillan, M. (2010). Recent perspectives on trade and inequality. Annual Review of Economics, 3, 261–289.
  • Katz, L. (2008). Skill-biased technological change. In S. N. Durlauf & L. E. Blume (Eds.), The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics. Palgrave Macmillan.
  • Rodríguez-Pose, A. (2018). The revenge of the places that don’t matter (and what to do about it). Cambridge Journal of Regions, Economy and Society, 11(1), 189–209.
entry.summary: What explains the rise of right-wing populism in high-income countries? This essay argues that technological change, not trade liberalisation, is the primary driver of manufacturing decline and the grievances fuelling populist politics.
